_about: The "Find your method" tree, read by tools/build.py (which checks it) and by the app's Find your method page. The first fork is the kind of question (a suit in meta.json), asked in everyday words (short, plain) with a real Question card as its example; the research term comes second (tag, term). Each branch then asks about the situation until it lands on a Method (method, an id in designs.json). next is a follow-up question, goto jumps to another kind of question, con is the constraint the answer stands for, time a time term, and a node's help teaches the research word behind its plain question. sources: what each zone's own categories are. The published classifications the tree can be viewed through, and the sources for the Method families, are in classifications.json.
intro: Have a research question but not sure how to study it? Answer a few plain questions. Each answer narrows the choice, until you reach the method that fits.

first.q: What do you want to find out?
first.help: Pick the one closest to your research question. The examples are real question cards from the game.

DESCRIBE.plain: How common something is, how much there is, or whether it is changing.
DESCRIBE.q: What do you want to describe?

options.label: One or a few unusual cases
options.hint: A patient, an accident or a failure nobody has seen before

options.label: A group you can take a sample from

next.q: Once, or again and again?

options.label: Once: how common is it right now?
Again and again: is it going up or down?
options.hint: The same measurement, taken the same way, over years

options.label: A group nobody can list in full
options.hint: Animals in a pond, people without a fixed address: count them from the overlap of two samples

options.label: Whole countries, regions or years
options.hint: You only have their averages, not data on single people

options.label: Published research itself
options.hint: Who cites whom: the shape of a research field

EXPLORE.short: What is going on, and why?
EXPLORE.plain: How people experience or do something, when nobody yet knows what matters.
EXPLORE.q: Where can you learn about it?

options.label: From people: their experience and habits

next.q: How much time can you spend with them?

options.label: Months: live among them and watch
Weeks: interview them, then look for patterns
Until a new explanation grows out of what you hear
One place or event, studied from every side
From experts who disagree
options.hint: Ask them in rounds until they agree

options.label: From watching people use a product
From what has already been written

next.q: Where is most of it written?

options.label: In scientific journals
In blogs, talks and company reports
From numbers and from people's stories
options.hint: One part explains or tests the other

ASSOCIATE.plain: Whether people with one thing more often have another, without proving that one causes the other.
ASSOCIATE.q: Do you already know which possible cause to look at?
ASSOCIATE.help: Researchers call the possible cause the exposure, and the result the outcome.

options.label: Cause unknown: test millions of genes, one by one
One possible cause and one result in mind

next.q: Is one of them rare?

options.label: The result is rare: 1 in 1,000 people or fewer

next.q: What is the possible cause like?

options.label: Brief, and it acts at once
options.hint: Something that happened in the hour or day before

options.label: Long-lasting, and easy to ask about or look up
options.hint: Start from the result, then look back at the cause

options.label: Costly to measure, from stored samples
options.hint: Measure it only for those with the result and a sample of the rest

options.label: The cause is rare: only a small group has it

next.q: Are there already records of that group?

options.label: Records exist: rebuild the group from them
No records: measure now, then follow them for years
Both the cause and the result are common

next.q: What data can you get?

options.label: One quick snapshot of many people
Only averages for whole countries or regions
Measurements of the same people over time

CAUSE.plain: Whether a treatment, policy or design change actually makes a difference.
CAUSE.q: Can you decide who gets the treatment or change?
CAUSE.help: Researchers call the treatment or change the intervention. If you decide who gets it, your study is an experiment; if not, it is observational.

options.label: I decide, and chance can pick, like a coin toss

next.q: Who does the coin toss pick?
next.help: Letting chance decide is called randomization. It makes the groups alike in everything except the treatment.

options.label: Single people

next.q: Anything special about your situation?

options.label: Nothing special: compare two groups, the standard way
They are visitors to a website or app
There are many treatments, and results come in over time
options.hint: Weak treatments are dropped and new ones added

options.label: Each person can try both, one after the other
options.hint: A lasting condition, and a treatment whose effect wears off

options.label: There is only one person
options.hint: Which treatment works best for this one patient?

options.label: Whole groups: schools, villages, clinics
options.hint: When people in a group would share or copy the treatment

next.q: Will every group get it in the end?

options.label: Every group gets it in the end; only the order is open
Not all get it; groups are services, like clinics
Not all get it; groups are places in nature or markets
options.hint: Fields, islands, shops

options.label: Several settings at once
options.hint: What each setting does, and how they work together

options.label: I decide, but only small changes in my own work
options.hint: Try it, measure, adjust, repeat

options.label: I can't decide: it already happened, or would be unfair

next.q: Did something else decide who got it?
next.help: Sometimes a rule, a date or nature splits people into groups for you. Researchers call this a natural experiment.

options.label: A score with a cut-off: above it you get it, below you don't
A change on a known date: a new law, policy or product

next.q: What can you compare with?

options.label: A similar group that did not get the change
Only the same place, measured many times before and after
A blend of similar places that did not get it
options.hint: Mixed to look like the changed place before the change

options.label: Something that nudges people towards it, and affects nothing else

next.q: What is the nudge?

options.label: Their genes
options.hint: Genes are handed out by chance at conception

options.label: Something else: distance, a lottery, a rule
Nothing decided it: the groups also differ in other ways

next.q: What do you have to work with?
next.help: Those other differences are called confounders. Whatever you pick, the analysis must adjust for them.

options.label: Detailed records: copy the trial you wish you could run
The result is rare: start from people who have it
The cause is brief: compare each person with themselves just before
Old records of a group that had it
Time to follow people for years
Nothing decided it, and there is only one case
options.hint: Test competing explanations, clue by clue

PREDICT.plain: Forecasting what comes next, or who it will happen to, without needing to know why.
PREDICT.q: What do you want to predict?

options.label: Who will get a result: an illness, a failure, a default

next.q: Do you have data from the past?

options.label: Past records show who got it
Past data, but a rare result and a costly predictor
No past data: measure now, then follow people
Where a trend is heading
How a system will behave, when you can't experiment on it
options.hint: A river, a city's traffic, an epidemic

options.label: What people will choose
Which tool or algorithm will do best
options.hint: Same tasks, same data, same scores

options.label: Whether it is worth the money

MEASURE.plain: Whether a test, device or questionnaire gives answers you can trust.

options.label: That a test finds what it should
options.hint: Compared with the best test there is, which researchers call the reference standard

options.label: That repeated measurements agree

next.q: Agree across what?

options.label: Different people or devices, in one place
Different laboratories, testing the same sample
That it really measures what it claims
options.hint: Does a stress questionnaire measure stress, or something else?

next.q: Does the questionnaire or scale exist yet?

options.label: No scale yet: build it and test it
No scale, and unclear what to ask: interview first
Scale exists: test its links to other measures
What people value
options.hint: Make them choose between options

options.label: What experts agree on, where nothing can be measured yet

EXPLAIN.short: Why does it work this way?
EXPLAIN.plain: The mechanism behind something: what must happen, and what follows from a theory.
EXPLAIN.q: How will you find out why?

options.label: Work it out with mathematics
options.hint: What must be true, every time

options.label: Build the system in a computer and run it
options.hint: When it is too complex to work out by hand

options.label: Experiment: change several settings together
Study it in real life

next.q: Do you already have an explanation to test?

options.label: No explanation yet: build one from what you observe
Rival explanations in one case: test them
One case, explanation in hand: study it from every side
A theory of how measurements should relate
From existing studies: what works, for whom, and why

BUILD.short: Can I make something that works?
BUILD.plain: Designing a device, tool or programme, and showing that it works and can be used.
BUILD.q: Where are you with what you're making?

options.label: Not started: does something like it exist already?
options.hint: Search patents, products and papers

options.label: Planning a big study: can it actually be run?
options.hint: A small trial run first

options.label: Building it

next.q: What do you need to find out?

options.label: Does it solve the problem for the people who use it?
Can people work out how to use it?
Which settings work best?
Comparing it with others

next.q: Compared on what?

options.label: Performance on the same tasks
Cost against benefit
Improving a process already in use
options.hint: Small, quick rounds of change

SYNTHESIZE.plain: Bringing together the research that already exists, instead of starting a new study.
SYNTHESIZE.q: What do you want from the existing studies?

options.label: One combined answer to a focused question

next.q: Anything special?

options.label: Nothing special: the standard review
I only have a few weeks
Many treatments to rank against each other
I can get each study's raw data
Many reviews already exist on it
Why it works, for whom, and in what situations
A map of what has been studied, and the gaps

next.q: Where is most of it written?

options.label: In scientific journals
In blogs, talks and company reports
The shape of a research field

next.q: Its roots, or what is active right now?

options.label: Its roots: works that are often cited together
options.hint: Needs years of citations to build up

options.label: What is active now: new papers that cite the same sources
options.hint: Works even on brand-new papers

options.label: What already exists, before you build

time._about: Time words shown as badges on the answers where timing decides the method ('time' on an option). Not a first question: time cuts across every purpose.

cross-sectional.name: Cross-sectional
cross-sectional.plain: A snapshot: everything is measured at one point in time.

longitudinal.name: Longitudinal
longitudinal.plain: The same things are measured again and again over time.

retrospective.name: Retrospective
retrospective.plain: Looks back at what already happened, in records or in people's memories.

prospective.name: Prospective
prospective.plain: Starts now and follows people forward in time.
